newsitem.title: USA: GOODWILL GAMES DOWNSIZING AND ADDING PRIZE MONEY.
newsitem.headline: GOODWILL GAMES DOWNSIZING AND ADDING PRIZE MONEY.

text.p: The Goodwill Games are downsizing, organisers said Tuesday, and hoping that $5 million in prize money will help lure the world's greatest athletes.
The 1998 Goodwill Games, to be held from July 19-Aug. 2 in New York City and vicinity, will feature half the sports offered at the 1994 Games in St Petersburg, Russia.

Competition will be in athletics, basketball, boxing, cycling (track), diving, figure skating, gymnastics, rhythmic gymnastics, swimming, synchronized swimming, triathlon, and volleyball (beach and indoor).
Sports that were eliminated included archery, rowing, weight lifting, yachting, canoe-kayak, judo, team handball, wrestling, water polo, soccer, speed skating and tae kwan do.

"We are trying to create a marketability as well as a TV-friendly product and that's why we picked the sports that we have," said Dr Harvey Schiller, president of Turner Sports, whose president, Ted Turner, founded the Games in 1986.
"These are the marquee sports and that we believe garner the most interest from the public," Schiller said.
More than 2,000 athletes competed in 24 different sports in St Petersburg. The next Games are expected to feature 1,300 athletes competing in 12 sports.
To boost the interest of top athletes, $5 million in prize money will be awarded, said Games president Michael Plant.
"We believe that that will provide enough motivation to bring the world's best here," said Plant, who would not reveal how the prize money would be allocated.
The first to sign up for the Games is Olympic hero Michael Johnson, who raced into the record books in Atlanta as the only man ever to win the 200 and 400 meters in the same Olympics.
"The good thing about the Goodwill Games in the past two that I have competed in is that they don't try to be like an Olympics," said Johnson.
"This is a separate and unique event," he said. "This is much more like a great sporting event of great international athletes."
